cse-2016-1-cs-13.approach: Recall each algorithm's worst-case input: reverse-sorted for insertion sort, any input for merge sort, and an already-sorted (or bad-pivot) input for quicksort.

steps.title: Insertion sort
steps.body: On a reverse-sorted array, element $i$ is compared with all $i-1$ earlier elements: $1+2+\cdots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=\Theta(n^2)$.

steps.title: Merge sort
steps.body: It always splits in half and merges in linear time, regardless of input: $T(n)=2T(n/2)+\Theta(n)=\Theta(n\log n)$ — worst case included.

steps.title: Quicksort
steps.body: If the pivot is always the minimum or maximum (e.g. sorted input with first-element pivot), each partition removes only one element: $T(n)=T(n-1)+\Theta(n)=\Theta(n^2)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Insertion sort's worst case is $\Theta(n^2)$, not $\Theta(n\log n)$; quicksort part is right.
Merge sort is $\Theta(n\log n)$ in every case, and quicksort's worst case is $\Theta(n^2)$.
Quicksort's $\Theta(n\log n)$ is its average/best case, not its worst case.
Correct: $\Theta(n^2)$, $\Theta(n\log n)$, $\Theta(n^2)$.

pitfalls: Quoting quicksort's average case $\Theta(n\log n)$ as its worst case.
cse-2016-1-cs-13.verification: Standard results: only merge sort (and heap sort) guarantee n log n in the worst case among these.

cse-2016-1-cs-14.approach: Adding the same constant c to every edge leaves the relative order of edge weights unchanged (so MST is unchanged), but adds c × (number of edges) to every path, which penalises paths with more edges — so shortest paths can change.

steps.title: Statement P
steps.body: Kruskal's algorithm depends only on the **sorted order** of edge weights. $w_1<w_2 \iff w_1+c<w_2+c$, so the order — and hence the (unique, since weights are distinct) MST — is unchanged. Also every spanning tree has exactly $|V|-1$ edges, so every tree's weight rises by the same $(|V|-1)c$. **P is true.**

steps.title: Statement Q — counter-example
steps.body: Let $A\to B$ directly have weight $5$, and $A\to C\to B$ have weights $2+2=4$. Shortest path: $A\,C\,B$ (4). Add $c=2$: direct edge becomes $7$, two-edge path becomes $4+4=8$. Now the direct edge is shorter. **Q is false.**

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: MST unchanged, shortest paths may change.
Q fails — a path with k edges grows by k·c, so paths with different edge counts change relative order.
P is true because the edge order (all that MST algorithms use) is preserved.
Q is false (see the counter-example).

pitfalls: Assuming shortest paths behave like MSTs; path lengths grow by c times the number of edges, which differs between paths.
cse-2016-1-cs-14.verification: Counter-example checked numerically: 5 < 2+2 fails before, 7 < 4+4 holds after.

cse-2016-1-cs-15.approach: mystery swaps only its local copies of the pointers; it never dereferences them, so nothing in main changes. Then trace main.

steps.title: What mystery does
steps.body: Inside `mystery`, `ptra` and `ptrb` are **local copies** of the addresses passed in. Swapping them (via `temp`) exchanges the local copies only; there is no `*ptra = …` or `*ptrb = …`, so the pointed-to integers are never modified. The swap vanishes when the function returns.

scene.caption: mystery(&a,&b): only local pointer copies swap; a, b unchanged

steps.title: Trace main
steps.body:
- Start: $a=2016,\ b=0,\ c=4,\ d=42$.
- `mystery(&a,&b)`: no change.
- `if (a < c)` is $2016<4$ → false, so `mystery(&c,&a)` is skipped.
- `mystery(&a,&d)`: no change.
- `printf` prints $a = 2016$.

scene.caption: a < c is false; a is still 2016

pitfalls: Treating mystery as a real swap of a and b (it would need *ptra/*ptrb assignments).
Even if it were a real swap, the condition would then be evaluated on the swapped values — read the code literally.
cse-2016-1-cs-15.verification: No statement in the program writes through a pointer, and a is never assigned after initialisation, so a = 2016.

cse-2016-1-cs-16.approach: S → aS | bS | ε lets you emit a or b any number of times in any order and then stop — that is exactly Σ*.

steps.title: Derive any string
steps.body: For any $w=c_1c_2\cdots c_k$ with $c_i\in\{a,b\}$: apply $S\to c_1S$, then $S\to c_2S$, …, then $S\to c_kS$, and finally $S\to\varepsilon$. So every string over $\{a,b\}$ (including $\varepsilon$) is derived.

steps.title: Nothing else
steps.body: Every production emits only $a$ or $b$, so no other strings can appear. Hence $L(G)=\{a,b\}^*$ (it is the right-linear grammar of the regex $(a+b)^*$).

Misses $ab\,a$ or $ba$, which are not of the form $a^n$, $b^n$ or $a^nb^n$.

cse-2016-1-cs-17.approach: Classify each problem: emptiness of an intersection of regular languages and CFG membership are decidable; CFG equivalence and TM emptiness are classic undecidable problems.

steps.title: I — decidable
steps.body: Regular languages are closed under intersection: build the product NFA of $N_1$ and $N_2$ and check whether any accepting state is reachable (graph search). **Decidable.**

steps.title: II — decidable
steps.body: CFG membership is decidable: convert to CNF and run the CYK algorithm in $O(|x|^3)$. **Decidable.**

steps.title: III and IV — undecidable
steps.body: Equivalence of two CFGs is undecidable (even $L(G)=\Sigma^*$ is undecidable). Emptiness of $L(M)$ for a TM is a non-trivial property of RE languages, so it is undecidable by Rice's theorem. **III and IV are undecidable.**

optionAnalysis.reason: I is decidable (product-automaton emptiness check).
II is decidable (CYK); only III of this pair is undecidable.
Correct: CFG equivalence and TM emptiness are undecidable.
II is decidable.

pitfalls: Confusing CFG emptiness/membership (decidable) with CFG equivalence (undecidable).
cse-2016-1-cs-17.verification: Matches the standard decidability table: for CFLs, membership and emptiness are decidable; equivalence is not.

cse-2016-1-cs-20.approach: With all processes arriving together, SRTF behaves exactly like SJF, which is provably optimal for average waiting time.

steps.title: SRTF = SJF here
steps.body: All processes arrive at time 0, so no new arrival can preempt; SRTF just runs jobs in increasing burst order — i.e. non-preemptive SJF.

steps.title: Why SJF is optimal
steps.body: If jobs run in order $b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n$, total waiting time $=\sum_{k}(n-k)\,b_k$. The largest multiplier $(n-1)$ should go to the smallest burst; any out-of-order adjacent pair can be swapped to reduce the sum (exchange argument). So shortest-first minimises average waiting time.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: equivalent to SJF for simultaneous arrivals, which minimises average waiting time.
Tiny-quantum RR interleaves all jobs, so every job waits roughly until near the end — far worse average waiting time than SJF.
A random order is optimal only by luck.
Priority ∝ burst length runs the longest job first — the worst ordering (LJF).

cse-2016-1-cs-20.verification: Example bursts 2, 4, 8: SJF waits 0+2+6 = 8 (avg 2.67); LJF waits 0+8+12 = 20.

cse-2016-1-cs-28.approach: Follow the rules to see which inputs are forced to share a value: every input not divisible by 5 collapses to f(1), every multiple of 5 collapses to f(5), and the two classes never mix.

steps.title: The rules preserve divisibility by 5
steps.body: $n\mapsto n/2$ and $n\mapsto n+5$ both keep "$5\mid n$" unchanged (5 is odd and coprime to 2). So multiples of 5 are only linked to multiples of 5, and non-multiples only to non-multiples.

steps.title: Non-multiples of 5 all share f(1)
steps.body: $f(1)=f(6)=f(3)=f(8)=f(4)=f(2)=f(1)$ covers $1,2,3,4$; $f(7)=f(12)=f(6)$; $f(9)=f(14)=f(7)$. In general an odd $n$ goes to $(n+5)/2<n$ for $n>5$, and even $n$ halves, so every non-multiple of 5 descends to one of $1,2,3,4$, all equal to $f(1)$.

steps.title: Multiples of 5 all share f(5)
steps.body: $f(5)=f(10)=f(5)$, $f(15)=f(20)=f(10)$, … every multiple of 5 descends to $5$. Hence $f$ takes at most two values, $f(1)$ and $f(5)$, and they may differ (e.g. $f(n)=1$ if $5\nmid n$, $2$ otherwise). Maximum $|R|=2$.
